title: Design a payment system
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, estimates, idempotency, ledger, PSP failure handling, reconciliation, refunds, security, sagas. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A payment system moves money from a payer to a payee safely: charge a card or bank account, record who owes what, pay out to merchants, and prove afterwards that every cent is accounted for. Stripe, Razorpay, PayPal, Adyen, Paytm/UPI apps. The key words are correctness, idempotency, ledger and reconciliation. Speed matters but being wrong costs real money and trust.

Functional requirements

  • Create a payment (charge) for an order; support cards, wallets, UPI/bank transfer.
  • Authorise then capture, refund (full or partial), void.
  • Payouts to merchants; fees and currency handling.
  • Webhooks/status for the merchant; payment history and receipts.
  • Reconciliation with banks and card networks.

Non-functional requirements

  • Never charge twice; never lose a successful payment; never show success for a failed one.
  • Strong consistency for money movements; auditability (immutable history).
  • Availability 99.99% for payment creation; graceful behaviour when a bank/PSP is slow or down.
  • Security and compliance: PCI DSS (card data isolated), encryption, fraud checks.

Decision gravity. Decide that the ledger (an append-only record of debits and credits) is the source of truth for money, and everything else (payment status, balances) is derived or must agree with it. One-way door: a wrong accounting model is nearly impossible to fix once real money has flowed through it.

Everyday analogy. Double-entry bookkeeping in a shop: every sale writes two lines in the book that must balance, and the book is never erased, only corrected with new lines.

Common interview traps.

  • Starting with "a payments table with a status column and a balance column that I update".
  • Forgetting refunds, failures and asynchronous bank responses.
  • Storing raw card numbers.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
POST /v1/payments
Authorization: Bearer sk_live_...
Idempotency-Key: 9c1f6a52-7d0e-4b9a-b6d1-0b2d4a1f1e11
{ "amount": 49900, "currency": "INR", "orderId": "o_9001",
  "paymentMethod": "pm_card_ab12",            // token from the card vault, never raw PAN
  "capture": false }
201 { "paymentId":"pay_77", "status":"REQUIRES_ACTION" | "AUTHORIZED" | "SUCCEEDED" | "FAILED",
      "amount":49900, "currency":"INR" }
409 Conflict -> same Idempotency-Key with a different body
402 Payment Required -> declined, with a decline code
POST /v1/payments/pay_77/capture   { "amount": 49900 }   -> 200
POST /v1/payments/pay_77/refunds   { "amount": 10000, "reason":"damaged" } -> 201 { "refundId":"rf_3" }
GET  /v1/payments/pay_77           -> status, amounts, ledger refs
POST /v1/payouts                   { "merchantId":"m_5", "amount": 1200000 }

Merchant webhook (we call them, signed with HMAC and retried with backoff):

POST https://merchant.example/webhooks/payments
X-Signature: t=1731150000,v1=5f2b...
{ "event":"payment.succeeded", "id":"evt_81", "data": { "paymentId":"pay_77", "amount":49900 } }

Amounts are integers in the smallest currency unit (paise, cents), never floats. The Idempotency-Key is mandatory on all mutating calls: same key plus same body returns the stored original response; same key plus a different body is rejected.

Industry example. Stripe's API popularised the Idempotency-Key header (keys retained 24 hours) and signed webhooks with retries for up to 3 days; Razorpay and Adyen follow close analogues.

Everyday analogy. A cheque with a unique serial number: depositing the same serial twice is recognised and refused.

Common interview traps.

  • Floating point money.
  • Webhook endpoints that are not idempotent (event delivered twice means double fulfilment).
  • Not saying how long idempotency keys are kept.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume a large PSP: 10M payments/day, peak 5x average, 1 KB per payment record, 5 ledger lines per payment.

Quantity Calculation Result
Payments avg 10M / 86,400 ~115/s
Payments peak x5 (sale events, festivals) ~600/s, design for 1,000/s
Ledger writes 600/s x 5 lines ~3,000 rows/s peak
Payment storage 10M x 1 KB x 365 ~3.6 TB/year
Ledger storage 10M x 5 x 200 B x 365 ~3.6 TB/year
Idempotency keys 10M/day x 24 h retention x 500 B ~5 GB live, trivially in Redis/DB
Webhooks ~3 events per payment 350/s avg, with retries ~700/s
PSP/bank latency card auth 500 ms to 3 s dominates user latency

What this tells you. Throughput is low compared with feeds or chat; a sharded relational database (Postgres/MySQL) is the right tool. The challenge is not QPS but correctness under partial failure: timeouts calling a bank, crashes between steps, duplicate callbacks. Latency is dominated by external parties you do not control.

Everyday analogy. A few thousand transactions per second is a modest crowd, but each one is a legal document.

Common interview traps.

  • Reaching for Cassandra/eventual consistency for ledger data.
  • Forgetting external latency dominates.
  • Sizing without retries and webhooks.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Payment service: owns the payment state machine; talks to PSPs/banks via adapters.
  • Idempotency layer: stores (merchant, key) -> request hash, response, status in the DB in the same transaction as the payment row.
  • PSP router: picks the acquirer/bank (cost, success rate, fallback), handles retries, circuit breakers per provider.
  • Ledger service: double-entry append-only records; the only place money balances change.
  • Card vault (PCI scope): tokenises card numbers; only this small, hardened service sees PAN data. Everything else handles tokens.
  • Fraud/risk engine: rules plus ML scoring, 3-D Secure triggering.
  • Webhook dispatcher, Reconciliation and Reporting pipelines on Kafka/warehouse.

Payment state machine

CREATED -> REQUIRES_ACTION (3DS/OTP) -> AUTHORIZED -> CAPTURED/SUCCEEDED -> (REFUNDED partially or fully)
   |                  |                     |
 FAILED            FAILED                 VOIDED
 + UNKNOWN (bank timed out; must be resolved by querying or reconciliation)

Decision gravity. The state machine includes an explicit UNKNOWN/PENDING state for "we sent the request and do not know what the bank did". Treating timeout as failure is the root of double charges and missing money. The alternative (assume failure) breaks catastrophically; it cannot be added later without reworking every caller.

Industry examples. Stripe: payments modelled as PaymentIntents with a state machine; their engineering posts on idempotency and on the ledger ("Ledger: stripe's system for tracking and validating money movement"). Uber and Airbnb have posted about their double-entry ledgers and payment orchestration.

Everyday analogy. A courier who might have delivered a parcel but lost the signature: you do not resend, you first call to ask.

Common interview traps.

  • Binary success/failure statuses.
  • Putting card numbers into general application databases or logs.
  • One PSP with no fallback or circuit breaker.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Idempotency: never charge twice

Why duplicates happen: client retry after timeout, user double-clicks, load balancer retry, message redelivery, webhook redelivery. The defence is an idempotency key supplied by the caller (client-generated UUID per logical operation).

Protocol on POST /payments:

  1. INSERT a row into idempotency_keys(merchant_id, key, request_hash, status='IN_PROGRESS') with a unique constraint on (merchant_id, key).
  2. If the insert fails (key exists): if request_hash differs return 409/422; if stored status='DONE' return the stored response verbatim; if IN_PROGRESS return 409 "request in flight" (or wait).
  3. Create the payment and talk to the PSP (passing the same key or payment id downstream so the PSP also dedupes).
  4. Store the response and mark DONE.
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  merchant_id BIGINT, idem_key TEXT, request_hash BYTEA,
  status TEXT, response JSONB, payment_id BIGINT,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (merchant_id, idem_key));
-- Step 1 is atomic thanks to the primary key; no race between concurrent retries
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (merchant_id, idem_key, request_hash, status)
VALUES ($1,$2,$3,'IN_PROGRESS') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

Downstream idempotency: pass your own paymentId as the PSP's reference/idempotency key; many acquirers dedupe on merchant reference. For UPI/bank rails use the transaction reference.

Keys are retained 24 hours to a few days (cleanup job), longer than any realistic retry window.

Decision gravity. Key scope and retention are API contract decisions (one-way once merchants integrate). Strong storage in the same DB transaction as the payment is the safest; Redis-only keys can lose data on failover (acceptable only with a DB fallback unique constraint on the payment's own reference).

Production incident pattern. Symptom: customers report two charges for one order after a payment gateway latency spike. Metric: rate of requests with repeated order ids and no idempotency keys, plus client retry counts. Cause: client SDK retried with a fresh key. Fix: derive the key from the order/cart id on the client side so retries reuse it, and add a server-side uniqueness check on (merchant, orderId) for active payments.

Everyday analogy. The serial number on a cheque.

Common interview traps.

  • Deduping on amount plus user within a window (false positives, e.g. two real purchases).
  • Generating a new key on every client retry.
  • Race between two concurrent identical requests (use the unique constraint, not check-then-insert).

The ledger: double-entry, append-only

Every money movement is recorded as a transaction consisting of at least two entries, total debits equal total credits. Accounts: customer, merchant, platform fees, PSP clearing, bank. Entries are immutable; corrections are new compensating entries. Balance = sum of entries (cached in a balances table updated in the same DB transaction).

Example: customer pays 499.00 INR, platform fee 2%.

Txn T1: payment captured
  DEBIT   psp_clearing_account       499.00
  CREDIT  merchant_pending_balance   489.02
  CREDIT  platform_fee_revenue         9.98
  (debits 499.00 = credits 499.00)
Txn T2: refund 100.00 (new entries, T1 untouched)
  DEBIT   merchant_pending_balance   100.00
  CREDIT  psp_clearing_account       100.00
CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
  entry_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  txn_id UUID NOT NULL, account_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  direction CHAR(1) CHECK (direction IN ('D','C')),
  amount BIGINT CHECK (amount > 0), currency CHAR(3),
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now());
-- Invariant checked per txn: SUM(amount) FILTER (D) = SUM(amount) FILTER (C)
-- Atomic: insert all entries and update balances in ONE database transaction

Properties:

  • Atomic: all entries of a transaction commit together (single shard, one DB transaction). Keep both sides of a txn on one shard (shard by account but design the txn between accounts on the same shard, or use sagas with an in-transit account if cross-shard).
  • Immutable: no UPDATE/DELETE on entries (enforce with permissions/triggers); audit-friendly.
  • Idempotent: the ledger txn has a unique txn_id/reference derived from the payment id and step, so a retried capture does not write twice.
  • Balance concurrency: updating balance = balance + x on a hot merchant row serialises writers; use sharded sub-balances or compute balances from entries and snapshot periodically.

Decision gravity. Double-entry ledger over a mutable balance column: you get invariants (sum is zero), history, easy audits and correction by compensation. Cost: more rows and complexity. Irreversible choice in practice, since all accounting reports build on it. When it breaks: huge hot accounts (platform fee account touched by every payment) become write bottlenecks, so batch or shard them.

Industry example. Stripe, Square (Books), Uber and Airbnb have published ledger designs; Modern Treasury and open-source TigerBeetle are specialised double-entry databases (TigerBeetle targets very high debit/credit throughput).

Everyday analogy. The shop's paper accounts book: write lines in ink; if you made a mistake, add a correcting line, never scratch out.

Common interview traps.

  • Updating a balance column without entries.
  • Ledger entries across shards without atomicity.
  • Using float or decimal inconsistently (use integer minor units).

Calling banks and PSPs: timeouts, retries, UNKNOWN

External call outcomes: success, definite decline, timeout/unknown. Strategy:

  1. Persist PENDING + intent before calling out (so a crash cannot lose the fact that we tried).
  2. Call with a per-call timeout (for example 5 s for authorisation) and the idempotency/reference key.
  3. On timeout: mark UNKNOWN; do not retry blindly with a new reference. Query the PSP by reference (status API) after short delays (2 s, 10 s, 1 min); if the PSP supports idempotent retry on the same reference, retry; else wait for the callback or reconciliation to settle.
  4. Webhooks/callbacks from the PSP are authenticated (signature, mTLS), deduplicated by event id, and applied through the state machine with allowed transitions only.
  5. Circuit breaker per PSP (open after, say, 50% failures over 30 s) and fallback routing to a second acquirer for new payments.
// Outbound call shape (pseudocode)
val intent = repo.savePending(paymentId)                 // durable first
val result = try { psp.authorize(ref = paymentId, amount, timeout = 5.seconds) }
             catch (e: TimeoutException) { PspResult.Unknown }
repo.apply(paymentId, result)                            // state machine decides next step

Asynchronous methods (UPI collect, net banking, 3DS) return REQUIRES_ACTION and finish later by callback; poll as a backstop since callbacks can be lost.

Decision gravity. Persist-intent-first plus UNKNOWN state is non-negotiable; routing and retry policy are tunable (reversible). Multi-PSP routing improves success rates (a few percentage points matter at scale) but multiplies integration and reconciliation work.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: customers charged, orders marked failed. Metric: count of payments in UNKNOWN older than 10 min; mismatch between PSP settlement file and ledger. Cause: callback lost during a deploy. Fix: status polling job and reconciliation.

Everyday analogy. You phoned the bank, the line dropped mid-sentence; you call back and ask "did that transfer happen?" before doing it again.

Common interview traps.

  • Retrying a charge with a new reference after timeout.
  • Marking timeouts as failed and releasing the order.
  • Trusting callbacks without verifying signatures or de-duplicating.

Reconciliation

Even good systems drift: lost callbacks, bank errors, manual adjustments. Reconciliation compares three sources of truth and flags differences:

  1. Your ledger/payments DB.
  2. The PSP/acquirer reports (daily settlement files: transaction id, amount, fee, status).
  3. The bank statement (what money actually arrived).

Process (daily or hourly): ingest files into a warehouse table, join on PSP reference, classify:

  • matched (amounts and status equal);
  • in our system only (we think success, PSP has nothing: investigate, maybe refund or retry);
  • in PSP only (money taken, we show failure: create the missing payment or refund customer);
  • amount mismatch (fees, currency conversion, partial capture).
SELECT COALESCE(l.psp_ref, p.psp_ref) AS ref, l.amount AS ours, p.amount AS theirs
FROM ledger_payments l
FULL OUTER JOIN psp_settlement p ON p.psp_ref = l.psp_ref
WHERE l.psp_ref IS NULL OR p.psp_ref IS NULL OR l.amount <> p.amount;

Automatic fixes for known patterns (late success callbacks); humans handle the rest with a work queue. Track break rate and time to resolve as KPIs; aim for under 0.01% unresolved. Recon also feeds merchant payout calculations: pay out only settled funds, with a rolling reserve for chargebacks.

Decision gravity. Treat reconciliation as a first-class product feature, not a back-office script. It is the safety net that lets other parts accept eventual consistency. Cheap to add early; extremely painful to retrofit after discrepancies accumulate.

Industry example. Every PSP runs continuous recon; Stripe's ledger posts describe automated checks that sum balances and compare to bank data, flagging any imbalance.

Everyday analogy. The shop owner compares the till receipts to the card machine slips to the bank statement at the end of the day.

Common interview traps.

  • No third-party source of truth: only reconciling the database with itself.
  • Hand-matching in spreadsheets.
  • Ignoring currency, fees and timing differences (T+1, T+2 settlement).

Refunds, payouts, security and fraud

Refunds are new payments in the opposite direction linked to the original: idempotent, limited to the captured amount minus prior refunds, each with its own ledger transaction. Card refunds take 5 to 10 days to appear for customers; a UPI reversal is quicker.

Payouts: batch by merchant on a schedule; use an outbox plus idempotent transfer requests; hold funds for a risk window; handle bank rejections by returning money to the merchant balance with a compensating entry.

Chargebacks (customer disputes through the card network): represent as ledger debits with evidence deadlines.

Security

  • PCI DSS: raw card data only in the vault (tokenisation); everything else sees tokens. Use hosted fields or SDKs so card numbers never touch merchant servers. Encrypt with envelope encryption (KMS/HSM keys), rotate keys.
  • TLS everywhere, signed webhooks, API key scoping, rate limits.
  • Fraud: velocity checks, device fingerprint, 3-D Secure step-up for risky payments, ML scores in under 100 ms (inline) plus post-payment review.

Decision gravity. Shrinking PCI scope by using tokens is a cost-saving, security-improving decision made early; undoing sprawl of card data afterwards is a multi-quarter project.

Everyday analogy. The vault in the bank: only the vault staff handle cash; everyone else works with deposit slips.

Common interview traps.

  • Logging request bodies that include card numbers.
  • Refunds not tied to the original payment (over-refund).
  • Skipping fraud and chargebacks in an "end to end" answer.

Consistency across services: sagas and the outbox

A payment touches orders, payments, ledger and notifications. Avoid distributed transactions (2PC) across services. Use a saga: a sequence of local transactions with compensations (void authorisation, refund, reverse ledger entries). Within the payment service use the transactional outbox: write the state change and the outgoing event row in one DB transaction; a relay publishes to Kafka; consumers (webhook sender, order service) are idempotent.

Databases: Postgres or MySQL with synchronous replica for money tables (synchronous_commit = on, quorum standby), serializable or at least repeatable-read plus explicit row locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) on accounts/payments being changed, and optimistic version columns to catch races.

BEGIN;
SELECT status FROM payments WHERE id=$1 FOR UPDATE;      -- serialise concurrent captures/refunds
-- check allowed transition, insert ledger txn, update payment, insert outbox event
COMMIT;

Decision gravity. Strongly consistent relational store for money, eventually consistent streams for everything around it. If you later shard the DB, pick a key (merchant id) that keeps a payment and its ledger entries together. Resharding is a one-way door.

Everyday analogy. The cashier finishes the till entry and puts the delivery slip in the same drawer, so one cannot exist without the other.

Common interview traps.

  • Publishing to Kafka before the DB commit (event for something that rolled back).
  • Two-phase commit across third-party APIs (impossible).
  • Last-write-wins on money rows.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Idempotency designed concretely: key, unique constraint, request hash, retention, downstream propagation.
  • Ledger as double-entry, append-only, atomic, with compensations.
  • State machine with PENDING/UNKNOWN and explicit allowed transitions.
  • Failure thinking: timeout after calling the bank, lost callback, duplicate webhook, crash between steps.
  • Reconciliation against PSP and bank files with a break-handling process.
  • Security: PCI scope, tokenisation, signatures, fraud checks.
  • Numbers: modest QPS, strong consistency, external latency dominance.
  • Seniors discuss multi-PSP routing, FX and fees, settlement timing, regulatory audit, and moving from monolith to sharded ledger.

Common interview traps.

  • Designing for scale instead of for correctness.
  • Using eventually consistent storage for balances.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Money systems optimise for correctness: integer minor units, strong consistency, audit trail.
  • Idempotency keys with a DB unique constraint, request hash and stored response prevent double charges; propagate references to the PSP.
  • Ledger = double-entry, append-only, atomic; derive balances; fix errors by compensating entries.
  • Persist intent before calling out; model UNKNOWN; resolve with status queries, callbacks and polling; use circuit breakers and fallback PSPs.
  • Reconcile ledger, PSP settlement and bank statements daily; treat breaks as measured work items.
  • Use the outbox and sagas for cross-service consistency, tokenisation to limit PCI scope, and fraud checks inline.
